pedagogy.summary: Nets make the 2-D↔3-D relationship visible and are the standard route to spatial visualisation in upper primary. The concept is best taught by folding and unfolding physical models and, crucially, by having children PREDICT whether an arrangement will fold before checking it. Structural reasoning is built by anchoring on a base face, tracking composites of faces (a 'line of four' wraps the sides of a cube), and mapping net features to solid features (shape→face, side→edge, point→vertex) so children move from judging by overall appearance to reasoning from properties.
bestPractices: Predict-then-fold: the child commits to a prediction ('will this fold into a cube?') and justifies it before physically folding to verify (Knight & Wright 2014).
Anchor a base face and fold the others up around it — this reduces the number and complexity of mental transformations and the load on working memory.
Build and track composites: a line of four squares wraps to form the sides of a cube; the remaining two cap top and bottom.
Use teacher questioning to map specific net features to solid features (shape→face, side→edge, point→vertex), shifting attention from holistic perception to structure.
Show many valid nets for the same solid (a cube has eleven) and contrast valid with invalid arrangements to break the single-prototype belief.
keyRepresentations: Physical fold-up nets (card, Polydron) folded and unfolded from the solid
The eleven cube nets chart; the T/cross prototype set beside non-standard nets
Base-face plus a 'line of four squares' composite
Face-to-face mapping diagram linking each net shape to a solid face
commonMisconceptions: Only the familiar T/cross net makes a cube (prototype-as-only-net; Mariotti 1989) — other valid nets are rejected and near-prototypes trusted.
Any arrangement with the right number of faces folds up — attends to face count, not arrangement.
Cannot predict the fold direction of an L-shape, so mis-assigns which faces meet — a face is thought 'stuck in the corner' or two squares that should be opposite are left adjacent.

learn.summary: Teach nets as the visible 2-D↔3-D relationship by having children PREDICT whether a flat arrangement of squares will fold into a cube, then fold to check. Build structural reasoning by anchoring on a base face, tracking composites (a 'line of four squares' wraps the cube's sides while the remaining two cap top and bottom, in nets that contain such a line), and mapping net features to solid features (each shape→a face; each fold line→an edge, while pairs of outer sides join to make the remaining edges; several corner points of the net meet at each vertex). The central goal is to move children from judging by whether a net 'looks like the usual one' to reasoning from structure — accepting unfamiliar valid nets (a cube has eleven), rejecting arrangements whose layout cannot close, and producing a genuinely new valid net.

activities.title: Predict then fold: does this arrangement close into a cube?
feedback: If the child rejects the staircase, fold it physically so they see it closes, then unfold several different valid nets from the same cube so they see there are many, not one (eleven in all).

If the child accepts the 2-by-3 block ('six squares, so it makes a cube'), fold it so they see squares land on the same face while other faces are left uncovered; mark a base face and track where each square lands.
Praise justification by imagined folding ('these two wrap round to opposite sides') over justification by resemblance ('it looks like the usual net').
activities.rationale: Committing to a prediction before verifying surfaces the child's reasoning and makes the folding the moment that confirms or overturns it. Contrasting a valid non-prototype net with an invalid six-square block directly targets the prototype-as-only-net and face-count misconceptions.
sourceClaims: Successful net-reasoners use imaged folding anchored to a base face and known composites (a 'line of four squares' wraps the cube's sides); the least successful rely on recognising the prototypical net rather than reasoning about structure, and inferences are rare without teacher support that maps net features to solid features. Potari & Spiliotopoulou categorised primary students' attention from holistic appearance to full geometric structure.
Mariotti (1989) found 10–13 year olds consistently found the prototypical T-shaped net by unfolding a cube but often believed it the ONLY possible net, neglecting symmetry to judge other nets.
learnerActions: Look at a flat arrangement of six squares and, before folding, commit to a prediction: 'will this fold into a closed cube?' and say WHY.

Fold the arrangement (physical card/Polydron cut-outs, or by folding a paper net) to check the prediction — treating the card as a stand-in for the ideal flat net and asking about the cube it would form, not about the card as an object.
Start with the familiar cross/T net, then meet an unfamiliar 'staircase' zig-zag (2-2-2) net and predict it before folding.
Fold the staircase and observe that it ALSO closes into a cube, with every face covered once and no face left open (allowing for slight gaps from card thickness).
Try a 2-by-3 block of six squares: predict, fold, and watch squares overlap onto the same face while other cube faces are left uncovered.
activities.intendedInsight: Whether a net closes into a cube is decided by the ARRANGEMENT of the squares, not merely by having six of them. Unfamiliar nets can be valid and prototype-looking blocks can fail.

activities.title: Anchor a base and track where every square lands
feedback: If the child names adjacent squares when asked which become opposite, re-anchor the base and narrate each square's destination as it folds; if the net contains a 'line of four', fold it to wrap the sides and place the last two as top and bottom.
If a face seems 'stuck in the corner', slow the fold and track that single square from flat to its final position.
Reinforce naming each square's destination out loud as it folds.
activities.rationale: Anchoring and composite-/destination-tracking are the strategies that distinguish successful from unsuccessful net-reasoners and lower working-memory load; L-shape fold-direction errors are a known difficulty that this activity directly rehearses.
sourceClaims: Successful net-reasoners use imaged folding anchored to a base face and known composites (a 'line of four squares' wraps the cube's sides); the least successful rely on recognising the prototypical net rather than reasoning about structure, and inferences are rare without teacher support that maps net features to solid features. Potari & Spiliotopoulou categorised primary students' attention from holistic appearance to full geometric structure.
learnerActions: Choose one square as the base face and fold the others up around it.

Where the net contains one (as in the cross/1-4-1 layout), identify the 'line of four squares' that wraps to form the sides, then place the remaining two as top and bottom; for other valid layouts such as the 2-2-2 staircase, track each individual square's destination from the base instead.
For an L-shape or line arrangement, predict the fold direction and name which two squares end up on OPPOSITE faces before folding.
After folding, point to the two squares that face each other across the cube and explain how you know they never touch.
activities.intendedInsight: Anchoring on a base face and tracking where each square lands (using composites like a line of four when the net has one) lets you predict which faces meet and which become opposite, reducing the amount you have to hold in your head at once.

activities.title: Make it fail, then make a new one
feedback: If the child can only reproduce the familiar net, show several unfolded valid nets from one cube to establish there are many.
Check the drawn net by folding it (physically or mentally, square by square) rather than by how it looks.

When mapping features, confirm explicitly that each shape→a face, each fold line or pair of joining outer sides→an edge, and that several net corners meet at each vertex (the cube has 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices).
activities.rationale: Requiring generation of a new valid net and face-to-feature mapping moves the child from holistic appearance to full geometric structure, and coordinates spatial visualisation with property-based reasoning.
sourceClaims: Property-based (spatial) reasoning and spatial visualisation must be coordinated by domain-specific knowledge to overcome the 'look' of a 2-D diagram; neither alone suffices, and the difficulty persists across grades 4–9.

Successful net-reasoners use imaged folding anchored to a base face and known composites (a 'line of four squares' wraps the cube's sides); the least successful rely on recognising the prototypical net rather than reasoning about structure, and inferences are rare without teacher support that maps net features to solid features. Potari & Spiliotopoulou categorised primary students' attention from holistic appearance to full geometric structure.
learnerActions: Starting from a valid net, slide ONE square to a new spot and predict whether it still folds into a cube; fold to check and describe what goes wrong when it fails.
Turn a valid net into a DIFFERENT valid net by moving just one square.
Draw a genuinely different arrangement of six squares that also folds into a cube (e.g. a 1-4-1 or 2-2-2 layout) and map each square to the cube face it becomes.

Map net features to solid features: each square→a face; each shared side (fold line)→an edge, and each pair of outer sides that join when folded→one more edge; several corner points of the net come together at each vertex (count them: 12 edges and 8 vertices on the cube).
activities.intendedInsight: Producing a new valid net and explaining why a moved square breaks or preserves the fold shows structural understanding that cannot be faked by matching the prototype.

activities.title: Extend the reasoning to other solids
feedback: If faces/edges/vertices don't match after building, return to the net and re-track the mis-folded face.
For the square-based pyramid, check that the four triangular faces fold up to meet at a single apex above the square base.
Encourage justifying rejections by what goes wrong in the fold, not by appearance.
activities.rationale: The curriculum covers nets of cubes, cuboids, prisms and pyramids; transferring the structural strategy across solids is the intended breadth and demonstrates the reasoning is not tied to one prototype.
sourceClaims: Nets of cubes, cuboids and other 3-D shapes are part of upper Key Stage 2 geometry in the English National Curriculum.
learnerActions: Draw and fold (mentally or physically) the net of a cuboid and a triangular prism, checking which faces connect.
Build a 3-D shape from its net and verify that all faces, edges, and vertices match.
Sketch a net of a square-based pyramid from a description or a 3-D model, transferring the base-and-fold reasoning from the cube.
Given several nets for one target solid, identify which fold correctly and explain why the others won't.
activities.intendedInsight: The same strategy — anchor a base, track how faces wrap, check faces/edges/vertices — applies beyond the cube to cuboids, prisms and pyramids.

constraints: Suitable for ages roughly 8–11 (upper Key Stage 2 geometry).
The predict-then-fold step is load-bearing: a prediction must be committed to and justified BEFORE folding, not after. Omitting the prediction reduces the task to observation.

Physical card/Polydron cut-outs have slight thickness and can be held, but they stand in for ideal flat (zero-thickness) faces; frame questions around the mathematical net and the cube it would fold into, not around whether the physical card can be picked up.

The 'line of four squares' composite applies to nets that contain such a line (e.g. the cross/1-4-1); it is not present in every valid net (e.g. the 2-2-2 staircase), where the general strategy is to track each square's destination from the base.

A static labelled net (each square tagged to the cube face it becomes, optionally with lift-the-flap or tap-to-highlight mappings) is a useful reference and reinforces face-to-face mapping, but it cannot be folded, so on its own it cannot provide the predict-then-fold experience.

A flat 2-D fold animation (drag squares, press fold, with overlap/missing-face flags) supports prediction and immediate close/fail feedback, but a flat animation can under-represent the spatial depth of the fold; pair it with physical folding or a rotatable model where possible.

A rotatable 3-D fold (watch faces swing up around a base, rotate the closing solid, see which squares become opposite) and hands-on physical card/Polydron both make the spatial fold concrete; they offer different experiences and either can carry the core mental action. Supporting non-standard nets on screen or in card lets 'only the T-net works' be disproved directly.

A 'which of these fold into a cube?' selection question is a useful CHECK after folding work; include a valid non-prototype net and an invalid six-square block as options. Recognition-only selection does not by itself elicit the folding reasoning or the production of a new net — pair it with asking the child to name opposite faces or draw a new valid net.
Spoken explanation of a prediction is a valuable prompt but is not a substitute for the spatial folding itself.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The claim that 'a cube has eleven distinct nets' is a well-known mathematical fact used in the source; it is stated as context, not re-derived here.

Legacy entries asserted 'dialogue cannot carry the spatial folding' and framed the 3-D interactive as uniquely 'ideal'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources, so they have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements in constraints. Physical folding, flat animation, and rotatable 3-D are presented as different means to the same mental action rather than a strict ranking.

The legacy row described the 2-by-3 block fold as 'two squares overlap, two faces missing'; the qualitative point (squares overlapping onto a face while other faces are uncovered) is sound, but the exact counts are a simplification and have been phrased qualitatively for learners.

The 'line of four squares' composite has been scoped to nets that contain it, to avoid conflicting with the 2-2-2 staircase example used elsewhere, which folds correctly without a straight line of four.

The source claims are drawn from the original row and support the general teaching principles (imaged folding, prototype misconception, coordination of spatial and property reasoning, curriculum placement); they do not demonstrate that any specific activity format above was empirically tested.

probeDeeper: Point to the two squares that end up facing each other on opposite sides of the cube — how do you know they don't touch?
If I slide this square from here to there, does it still fold into a cube? Why?
A cube has eleven different nets — can you turn your net into another valid one by moving just one square?
Here is an arrangement of six squares that does NOT fold into a cube — what goes wrong when we fold it?
assess.correctAnswer: Accepts the cross and the staircase as valid and rejects the 2-by-3 block; justifies by imagined folding anchored to a base face — tracking which squares wrap to the sides and which two become top and bottom / opposite faces, not by resemblance to a 'usual' net — and draws a fourth genuinely different valid net (e.g. a 1-4-1 or 2-2-2 arrangement) mapping its squares to cube faces.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes only the familiar cross/T net makes a cube ('that's how a cube is always made'), so rejects valid non-standard nets and trusts anything resembling the prototype
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fold the rejected staircase physically to show it closes, then unfold several different valid nets from the same cube so the child sees 'there are eleven, not one'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects the valid staircase net and accepts near-prototype look-alikes, justifying by resemblance rather than folding

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges by the number of faces, not their arrangement — 'it has six squares so it must fold into a cube'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fold the block so the child sees two squares overlap and two faces missing; mark a base face and track where each square lands
errorPatterns.distractor: The 2-by-3 block of six squares — 'six squares, so it makes a cube'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts the 2-by-3 rectangular block of six squares

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot predict the fold direction of an L-shape or line, so mis-assigns which faces meet — thinks a face is 'stuck in the corner' or that two squares that should be opposite end up adjacent
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor a base and fold the 'line of four' to wrap the sides, then place the last two as top and bottom, narrating each square's destination
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked which faces become opposite, names adjacent squares, or loses track of a face while folding the staircase

responseLevels.gap: Judges nets by whether they look like the usual cube net; accepts or rejects on appearance and cannot say which faces meet.
responseLevels.full: Anticipates the fold by anchoring a base and tracking composites, identifies opposite faces, explains why an invalid arrangement fails, and generates a genuinely different valid net — transferring the reasoning to the square-based pyramid.
responseLevels.partial: Correctly folds the familiar nets and names faces one at a time, but cannot coordinate a composite (e.g. predict the L-shape's fold) or reliably produce a new valid net — listing the squares without tracking how they act on each other.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are three flat arrangements of six squares: the usual cross-shaped net, a 2-by-3 block of six squares, and a 'staircase' zig-zag net. For each one, tell me whether it will fold into a closed cube and how you know — point to which square becomes the top and which two faces end up opposite each other. Then draw me a different arrangement of six squares that also folds into a cube.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child reasoning structurally accepts the unfamiliar staircase and rejects the six-square block because folding makes two faces overlap and leaves two missing; a child reasoning by appearance does the opposite — trusting the block because 'six squares equals a cube' and rejecting the staircase because it doesn't look like the usual net. Requiring them to name opposite faces and to PRODUCE a new valid net cannot be faked by prototype-matching.
